claims.text: In CrFeCoNiX alloys, formation and persistence of a protective oxide above 900 °C is governed by selective oxidation of the X element.
When X is Al, the alloy forms a slow-growing alumina scale.
The alumina scale formed by the Al-containing alloy is coherent and adherent.
The alumina scale retards further oxidation of the Al-containing alloy.
CrFeCoNiMn and CrFeCoNiSi form less coherent and more rapidly growing oxides than the Al-containing alloy.
Oxides on the Mn- and Si-containing alloys are more prone to cracking and spallation.
The controlled intervention is to replace Mn or Si with Al while keeping processing and other alloy constituents comparable.
The proposed comparison uses exposure at approximately 950 °C in dry air for 100–200 hours.
Thermal cycling is proposed to assess oxide-scale adhesion under strain generated by temperature fluctuations.
The relevant structural mediator is formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer rather than discontinuous or mismatched Mn- or Si-derived scales.
Al selectively oxidizes to thermodynamically stable Al2O3.
Al2O3 has a low growth rate and a favorable thermal-expansion match with the alloy.
Mn- or Si-derived oxides grow more rapidly and develop internal stresses that cause cracking and spallation.
After prolonged high-temperature exposure, the Al-containing alloy is predicted to retain a coherent and protective alumina scale.
Under the same exposure, the Mn- and Si-containing alloys are predicted to exhibit cracked or spalled oxide layers that compromise protection.
The hypothesis is asserted to apply to single- or multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions in oxidative or corrosive atmospheres above 900 °C.
Secondary-phase formation or extreme composition changes may alter the proposed oxidation behavior.

Failure of the Al-containing alloy to form a continuous, adherent alumina scale, or cracking and spallation comparable to the Mn- or Si-containing controls, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.
